questions.q: What does HTTP request smuggling exploit?
o: A TLS version gap between the front-end and the back-end
Front-end and back-end disagreeing on each HTTP/1 request's end
A CORS policy that copies any Origin into Access-Control
A gzip decoder treating leftover bytes as another request
questions.x: Many apps sit behind a proxy that forwards several HTTP/1 requests on one back-end connection. That only works if both sides agree where each request stops. Hidden leftover bytes can then become the start of the next request.
questions.h: HTTP/1 can describe body length in more than one way. What goes wrong if the two servers pick different rules?

questions.q: Which two HTTP/1 headers can describe how long the body is?
o: Content-Type and Transfer-Encoding
Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
Accept-Encoding and Content-Length
Host header and Transfer-Encoding
questions.x: Content-Length is an exact byte count. Transfer-Encoding: chunked sends pieces and ends on a zero-size chunk. If both headers are present and the two servers disagree, extra bytes can be hidden from one of them.
questions.h: One header is a total byte count. The other sends the body in chunks. Name both.

questions.q: In the CL.TE smuggling variant, which server uses which header?
o: Front-end uses Transfer-Encoding. Back-end uses Content-Length.
Front-end uses Content-Length. Back-end uses Transfer-Encoding.
Both servers use Content-Length but they pick different values.
Both servers use Transfer-Encoding with a malformed TE token.
questions.x: CL.TE means the front-end trusts Content-Length and the back-end trusts Transfer-Encoding. TE.CL is the reverse. TE.TE is when both speak chunked but one can be confused by a weird Transfer-Encoding header.
questions.h: CL and TE are abbreviations for the two length headers. Map each abbreviation to the server that uses it in CL.TE.

questions.q: Consider these claims about request smuggling. (1) It only affects HTTP/2 connections. (2) Both servers must use the same length header. (3) Smuggled bytes cannot reach another user's request. Which option is correct?
o: Only the first claim is true
None of these statements are true
Only the first two claims are true
Only the third claim is true
questions.x: The ambiguity is an HTTP/1 framing problem. The attack needs the two servers to disagree, not to agree. Leftover bytes on the shared back-end socket can prefix another user's next request.
questions.h: Which of those three claims is actually how HTTP/1 smuggling works?

questions.q: What can leftover smuggled bytes do to another user?
o: They can only change the attacker's own session cookies
They can prefix that user's next request on the shared socket
They only matter if both requests arrive in the same millisecond
They can rewrite response headers but never the request line
questions.x: Impact includes skipping front-end rules, poisoning another user's request or response, stealing tokens, poisoning caches, and reaching privileged paths the front-end would not have allowed on its own.
questions.h: The extra bytes stay in the back-end buffer. What happens when the next real request arrives on that same connection?
